subject: Agriculture
title: Photosynthesis and Food
description: A quick, practical guide to Photosynthesis and Food.

hook.text: Every calorie you eat started as sunlight. Plants are the only machines that turn light into food.

buildup.text: Chlorophyll in leaves captures photons and uses their energy to split water and fix carbon dioxide.

discovery.text: The process produces glucose—the basic sugar from which all plant tissues, starch, and oils are built.

twist.text: Photosynthesis is only about 1–2% efficient. Most sunlight is reflected, transmitted, or lost as heat.

climax.text: Despite low efficiency, photosynthesis powers all agriculture—and nearly all life on Earth.

punchline.text: Plants catch just 1% of sunlight. That 1% feeds the world.

quiz.question: How efficient is photosynthesis at converting sunlight to plant energy?

details.summary: Photosynthesis is the biochemical process by which plants convert sunlight, water, and CO₂ into sugars that feed the world. This topic covers light reactions, the Calvin cycle, and how improving photosynthetic efficiency could dramatically increase crop yields.
details.whyItMatters: All food ultimately comes from photosynthesis. Even small improvements in photosynthetic efficiency could add billions of tons to global crop production annually.
takeaways: Photosynthesis captures less than 2% of incoming solar energy in most crops
The Calvin cycle converts CO₂ into simple sugars using energy from light reactions
Research projects aim to boost crop photosynthesis by up to 40% through engineering

faq.question: How does photosynthesis relate to food production?
faq.answer: Every calorie humans consume traces back to photosynthesis. Plants use sunlight to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose, which is then stored as starch, fat, or protein in seeds, fruits, and roots that become our food.

faq.question: Can scientists improve photosynthesis to increase crop yields?
faq.answer: Yes. Projects like RIPE (Realizing Increased Photosynthetic Efficiency) are engineering faster enzymes, reducing photorespiration losses, and optimizing light capture to boost the efficiency of photosynthesis by 20–40% in staple crops.
